title: Pentagon Drafts New Nuclear Strategy for Regional Wars With China or Russia
excerpt: The Defense Department is developing plans that would deploy tactical nuclear weapons in a regional conflict, shifting away from the all-or-nothing deterrence model of the Cold War.
body:
• The Pentagon is drafting a new nuclear employment strategy focused on using tactical nuclear weapons in a regional conflict with China or Russia, according to NBC News citing multiple sources.
  • The shift reflects a "two-nuclear-peer" environment where the U.S. must simultaneously deter both China and Russia — a scenario without precedent in American defense planning.
  • The 2026 National Defense Strategy notably omitted explicit mention of extended deterrence, instead stating allies would "take primary responsibility" for their own defense.
  • Arms control experts warn the strategy could lower the threshold for nuclear use, while advocates argue it fills a dangerous gap in U.S. deterrence capabilities.

The Pentagon is quietly drafting a new nuclear weapons strategy designed for a scenario American defense planners spent decades hoping to avoid: a regional war with China or Russia where tactical nuclear weapons could be deployed, according to NBC News, citing multiple sources familiar with the planning.

The strategy represents a significant departure from the Cold War-era framework of mutual assured destruction, which treated nuclear weapons primarily as tools of last resort against an all-out attack. Instead, the new approach envisions a spectrum of nuclear options calibrated for limited regional conflicts — a concept that has gained urgency as both Russia and China expand their arsenals of lower-yield weapons.

The Two-Peer Problem

At the heart of the strategic rethink is what defense officials call the "two-nuclear-peer" challenge. For the first time in its history, the United States faces two major nuclear-armed adversaries simultaneously expanding and modernizing their arsenals.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=7V0V1y86bbs

China has rapidly grown its nuclear stockpile, with the Pentagon estimating Beijing aims to amass over 1,500 warheads by 2035 — more than tripling its current arsenal. Russia maintains roughly 3,500 nuclear weapons when nonstrategic weapons are counted, including a growing stockpile of lower-yield warheads unrestricted by treaties.

A Congressional Strategic Posture Commission report warned that the current U.S. nuclear program of record is "necessary but not sufficient" to address this dual threat, recommending expanded procurement of long-range standoff weapons, B-21 bombers, and Columbia-class submarines.

Tactical Nuclear Shift

The new strategy's focus on tactical — or "nonstrategic" — nuclear weapons reflects a debate that has intensified since Russia's invasion of Ukraine and its repeated nuclear threats. Russia has pursued what experts call a theory of nuclear "de-escalation," using the threat of limited nuclear strikes to prevent NATO from intervening in regional conflicts.

The U.S. Air Force has begun shaping policy around "conventional and nuclear integration," treating the two as points on a spectrum rather than separate categories. Geographic combatant commanders would participate in nuclear battle planning and nominate targets — a level of field-level involvement that some arms control advocates find alarming.

"One of the misperceptions about Russian nuclear strategy is that it takes advantage of lower-yield nuclear weapons that the United States does not have," wrote analysts Michael Kofman and Anya Loukianov Fink. "This appears nowhere in Russian military writings or deliberations."

Extended Deterrence Under Strain

The strategy emerges against a backdrop of shifting U.S. commitments to allies. The 2026 National Defense Strategy did not explicitly mention extended deterrence — the decades-old promise to defend allies with American nuclear weapons if attacked. Instead, it stated that allies and partners would "take primary responsibility" for their own defense with "critical but more limited U.S. support."

That language has alarmed some members of Congress and allied governments. A July Congressional Research Service report noted growing concerns about "friendly proliferation" — the possibility that U.S. allies, uncertain of American guarantees, might pursue their own nuclear weapons programs.

South Korea and Japan have both seen domestic debates about nuclear acquisition intensify in recent years, driven partly by North Korea's expanding arsenal and partly by questions about the reliability of U.S. security commitments.

The India Factor

For India, the evolving U.S. nuclear posture carries implications beyond the bilateral relationship. As a nuclear-armed state that shares borders with China and maintains a no-first-use doctrine, India watches closely as the global nuclear order shifts. Any lowering of the nuclear threshold between the U.S. and China could reshape the strategic calculus across the Indo-Pacific.

India's own nuclear modernization — including submarine-launched ballistic missiles and multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles — reflects its assessment of a more dangerous nuclear environment.

What Comes Next

Arms control advocates warn that developing dedicated tactical nuclear capabilities could accelerate a nuclear arms race rather than prevent conflict. But proponents argue that failing to match Russia's and China's theater-range nuclear options leaves a dangerous gap in deterrence.

The Pentagon has not publicly confirmed the details of the strategy, which remains classified. Its development, however, signals that American defense planners are preparing for a world where nuclear weapons are no longer merely the weapons of last resort — but instruments of regional military strategy.

nri_angle: The shifting U.S. nuclear posture has direct implications for India's strategic calculus as a nuclear-armed neighbor of China in an increasingly multipolar nuclear world.
